title: Unify Version 2
description: A life-improvement app for people who, frankly, don't know how to manage their life. Write down your problems, turn them into goals, and turn the goals into steps. Sign in with Google and it's on your phone and your computer.

sections.content: Unify. Because you don't know how to manage your life.
People ask us, "How does Unify know I can't manage my life?" And the answer is simple. You're reading this.
Our competitors say their apps help you manage your life. We don't think you can. That's the difference.

Unify is for everyone. More specifically, it's for a married man with children who, several times a year, needs to get ten people to do something inside forty-eight hours. If that isn't you, Unify will still work. You'll just have fewer people to disappoint.
Part 1: The High Cost of Dwelling

Cognitive overload is real, and almost nobody acknowledges it. The people who were running their lives twenty years ago tend to assume the present works the way theirs did. It doesn't. Twenty years ago a problem was a flat tyre. Today a flat tyre comes with an app, a subscription, and a short survey about the flat tyre.

Your dad had one password. It was the dog's name. You have a hundred and forty, and the dog now has two-factor authentication. You have a wife, children, and a group chat of ten people that you started, and which is now your fault.

Your brain handles this the only way it knows how. It dwells. It loops the problem through working memory, again and again, trying to solve it with brute-force worry. Your brain is a poor office manager, and it has been given a very large office.

Unify breaks the loop by making you write the problem down, one at a time, and file it: which part of your life it lives in, and how it makes you feel. The worry stops being a feeling and starts being a form. You are very good at forms. You've been filling them in your whole life.
Unify offers nineteen emotions to choose from, including Disapproving, Disassociated and Physical Pain. Happy is not one of them. You are here for a reason.

Some people feel that writing their problems into a computer is cheating. It isn't. It's the same as a notepad or a diary. Nobody accuses a shopping list of cheating at shopping. Your grandmother kept a diary. That wasn't weakness. That was external storage. She just had a worse interface.
Part 2: Quantifying the Struggle

In the heat of the moment, every problem feels like a catastrophe. A missed email feels just as stressful as a missed mortgage payment, because the emotional brain struggles to tell the difference in scale. We've made it easy:

content: ★★★  The email was about the mortgage payment.

sections.content: Every problem in Unify gets a difficulty, from one to five, which forces your logical brain to step in and ask whether this is a disaster or a nuisance. Level one is "Fixable now." Level four is "Fixable with the right resources and cooperation from others." Level five is "I do not know how to fix this problem." Our research shows these last two are the same level.

We're not asking you to be a Stoic. Marcus Aurelius ran the Roman Empire and he still needed a journal. He did not have a shared to-do list, and his son was Commodus. You can have feelings. The trouble is what a freak-out costs, and when. A freak-out on day one of a plan costs you a day. A freak-out at month eleven costs you eleven months. Managing your emotions isn't about being calm. It's about protecting the trajectory.
Part 3: The Memory Trap

We all assume we'll remember our lessons. We don't. The insight you gain on a stressful Tuesday is usually gone by a relaxing Saturday. We know this because we wrote it down on a Tuesday. On Saturday we read it back and did not recognise the handwriting. It was typed.

Memory isn't stored in one place. Some of yours is in your head. The rest is in a drawer, a group chat, and a receipt in the footwell of the car. Some experiences need to be caught at the moment they happen and processed later, when you're able to.

So Unify keeps a journal, and it doesn't wait for you to feel like writing in it. Every time you tick off a step, Unify asks what went well, and what you'd do differently. Tick off "take the bins out" and it will ask. Most people say nothing. They are wrong. There is always something.

Then there's Probe. Describe what's happening in your own words, and Probe finds the last time you wrote about something like it, and what came of it. It also notices what keeps coming back, which problems have no plan, and which goals have gone quiet. Probe has read everything you've ever written. It is not judging you. It is just very well informed.
Delete something and Unify remembers that you deleted it. Not what it was. Just that you deleted it, and when. Like a good friend.
Part 4: From Problems to Steps

Solving problems returns you to zero. That sounds modest. It isn't. Bad things rarely come from one problem. They come from several small ones arriving at once. Bad mood, plus running late, plus tired, equals car crash. Remove any one of them and it's just a Tuesday.

Not using Unify is like skipping the low-level enemies on the way to the boss fight. Nobody has ever been killed by the dragon. They were killed by the dragon plus the four skeletons they didn't bother with on the way in. The skeletons don't do much damage individually. That's why you ignore them. That's why they win.

In Unify, you gather a few problems into one goal: what you'll do about them, why it matters, and the first steps, one per line. When the goal is done, Unify offers to mark its problems resolved. They go into your history, where you can visit them, the way you'd visit an old enemy who is now very small.

Earlier versions of Unify included the Harada Grid, which breaks a five-year vision into eight sub-goals and sixty-four daily habits. Shohei Ohtani used a Harada Grid to become the best baseball player in the world. We used it zero times. It has been retired, with honours. Here it is anyway. Try it. You won't use it either.
Part 5: Your People

When you were younger, you lone-wolfed it. The only person looking out for your problems was you, and frankly, you were busy. Then you got married, had children, and acquired a degree of influence. Now your problems have other people in them.

Say you're going out of town for the day. Your wife has five places she wants to go. You can't think of one. You get home and remember everything you meant to buy. This happens roughly once a month, and you have never once remembered on the way there.

So Unify has sessions. Pick the steps you want done today, put them in order, and send her the link. She adds her five places. You sort the list together in the car, which is the closest most couples ever come to a five-year plan. Your problem-solving carries on, uninterrupted, through the craft markets.

Now say you have ten people and forty-eight hours. This happens to you more often than to most people, because you are, let's be honest, a person of some influence. Without a plan, ten people become a committee by lunchtime. Somebody has an opinion about the ladder. By mid-afternoon two of them aren't speaking, and nothing has been built.

With a shared session, everyone rocks up, opens the link, grabs a task and gets to work. Nobody needs to talk. Everyone plays to their strengths. The person with the opinion about the ladder is given the ladder.
Anyone with the link can tick things off and add to it. What they add waits for you to keep or discard. If it was added by your wife, we do not recommend discarding it.
Part 6: Sovereign Data

True self-analysis requires a sanctuary. You can't be honest about your financial fears or your personal failings if you think someone is reading over your shoulder. You sign in to Unify with your Google account, and what you write is kept in your account, for you, on your phone and your computer.
Probe runs a language model, and it runs it on your phone. Nothing you write is sent anywhere to be read. It is the most discreet thing you own, and it has read the most.
You can clear your browser history, and Unify won't mind. It isn't in there. We cannot stress enough how much it is not in there.
Ask Unify
Unify already has an AI that reads everything you write. Now it also has one that reads nothing. Between them, perfect balance. Go ahead. Ask it anything.
Unify is in the business of Tuesdays.
